badsonstudios
body:
Closes #216

## What this does

A session that came back with the app and hasn't been resumed yet — a
**suspended** card — used to draw its "Session suspended / Resume" panel and
nothing else. No header. So the gesture the workspace documents everywhere
else, **double-click a session's header to fill the workspace with it**, had
nothing to land on for that one card: `Ctrl+Shift+M` worked, the mouse didn't,
and the manual had to tell you so.

It has a header now: the session's name, its colour and language badge, and the
word *suspended*. Double-click it and it maximizes; double-click again and the
workspace goes back exactly as it was — the same behaviour every other card has.

Nothing else was added to it. The header carries **no buttons** — the two
things a suspended card can actually do, **Resume** and **Close**, are already
the buttons in the middle of the card. And maximizing one does **not** wake it
up: it stays suspended, with its Resume button, until you press that.

Under the hood the two headers now share their styling and their double-click
handler rather than having a second copy of the row (a copy is the thing that
drifts), and the card's identity resolves from the live session when there is
one and from the card record when there isn't — so a card restored at boot
never flashes a grey border before its real colour arrives.

## What to test

Automated tests already cover (please don't repeat): that the header exists on
a suspended card with the right name, badge, accent and word; that it has no
buttons; that double-click maximizes and un-maximizes; that it survives the
card being unmounted and re-mounted; that none of it resumes the session
(8 unit tests in `SessionGrid.suspended-header.test.tsx`); and the whole
journey end-to-end — pop out, close the window, double-click the card that
comes home — in `e2e/layout-modes.spec.ts`. The full card/header e2e
regression set (session, task-label, rules, sounds, document-peek, diff,
urgency, feed-restore-position, popout-dock-back) was run green.

- [ ] 1. Open two sessions. Pop one out (**⤢** in its header), then close that
      window with its **X**. The card comes home saying **Session suspended** —
      and it should now have a proper header above the panel: the session name,
      its colour down the left edge, its badge, and *suspended* on the right.
- [ ] 2. **Double-click that header.** The workspace should fill with that one
      card, and the other session should fold into the Collapsed strip at the
      bottom.
- [ ] 3. **Double-click it again.** Both cards should be back exactly as they
      were.
- [ ] 4. Through all of it the card must still say **Session suspended** with
      its **Resume** button — maximizing a card is a request about the
      workspace, not about the session. Nothing should have restarted.
- [ ] 5. Now press **Resume**. The session starts normally and the card's real
      header (with its ⌄ / ⤢ / ⋯ controls) takes over. Double-click that too —
      the gesture should be unchanged from before this PR.
- [ ] 6. Sanity check on a normal card: double-click the **task label** in a
      live header — it should still just start editing, not maximize.

## Out of scope — reported, not fixed

- **The `ended` / never-started card still has no header.** A session that
  crashed or refused to start lands on a different branch, which also renders
  the overlay alone — so the same double-click gap exists there. It is a
  separate state with a separate status word, and #216 named the suspended one;
  the pieces this PR extracted make it a small follow-up. Worth a ticket.

### New hero shots

The README still led with a photograph of the **blue robot mascot retired a week ago** — so the first thing anyone saw was a product that no longer exists.

Three shots of the real board on v1.6.x replace it: **Meters**, **Focus**, and **the kitsune**. The kitsune one catches it on **one tail** under "running low!" — Weekly at 13% left — so the gauge is legible in the photo rather than only in the caption.

Cropped from 6144×8160 phone frames (board was ~¼ of the picture) to 1050×1400 at ~220KB, matching the existing assets. The alternative was 19MB of README.

`sprocket.jpg` deleted. `timer.jpg` kept on disk but no longer referenced.

### A claim that stopped being true today

> ~~After that the board polls on its own over Wi-Fi and **the computer can be off**~~

That was accurate while the board renewed its own login — which is precisely what was logging people out of Claude Code. It now says the board tops itself up from your computer, pauses after a few hours without it, and explains why.

### The second board, honestly

Named as **coming soon** with an explicit *"don't buy one yet"*: pins and driver are in the firmware, but no image is published and the flasher only offers the LCD board. Anyone buying one today would have nothing to install.

PRODUCT.md's evidence section updated to match.

author: stxkxs
body:
`scripts/crd.sh freshness` and `scripts/xrd.sh freshness` exit 2 to mean "the
pin is behind" — a verdict the steps below turn into a filed drift issue
carrying the report and the re-vendor command. That verdict never reached them.

GitHub invokes a `run:` block as `bash -e {0}`, so errexit is already on when
the script starts, and `set -uo pipefail` does not clear it. A bare invocation
exiting 2 terminated the step at that line, before `code=$?` executed. With the
output unset, every `if: steps.freshness.outputs.code == ...` step below was
skipped — no issue filed, no report, no remediation text, only a red run whose
log ends at the command that produced the answer. A check that reports "behind"
and nothing else is the one a reader consults instead of checking whether the
mechanism works.

Initialising `code=0` and capturing through `|| code=$?` puts the command on the
left of a `||` list, which errexit exempts, so a 2 is captured rather than
fatal. The job still fails while a pin is behind; the drift issue is filed
alongside it.

`xrd-freshness.yaml` carried the same construction while its pin was current,
so its verdict path went green on a run that exercised none of it.

author: anveio
body:
## What

Fail-loudly instrumentation for the WebTransport port, ahead of the Effect rewrite — we need the error surface trustworthy so the rewrite lands against a known good state.

- **`@guardian/chunkies-transport-web`**: new `onError(error, context)` option. Every absorbed failure reports with `error.op` (`transport.dial` / `transport.session`), `error.phase` (`mint`, `handshake`, `handshake-late`, `open`, `uplink`, `datagram`, `downlink-stream`, `downlink-datagram`, `closed`), `transport.endpoint`, and `error.after_ms`. Abandoned dials watch their `ready`/`closed` rejections instead of leaking them as anonymous `unhandledrejection` noise. Self-initiated teardown reports nothing.
- **`@guardian/telemetry`**: `shapeOf` folds `WebTransportError.source`/`streamErrorCode` into the message and falls back to the error name — WebKit's WebTransportErrors carry empty messages, which today collapse into one useless signature.
- **WUM**: wires `onError` → `reportError` (general error lane, filter server-side on `error.op`), adds `wum.attempt` to `wum.redial`.

No behavior change to dialing, backoff, or teardown — reporting only.

## Why

iOS is at 0/13 connected over 14 days. Prod analytics show every iOS dial timing out at the 10s handshake deadline, but the causal error only ever reached the HUD log (`host.ts` catch), and the only beaconed evidence was empty-message `WebTransportError` unhandledrejections. After this lands, iOS sessions will report `handshake` timeouts and — critically — the `handshake-late` rejections carrying WebKit's actual failure reason.

## Testing

- `chunkies-transport-web`: 17 tests incl. new "errors as data" contract suite against the scripted fake (all phases, late rejections, self-close silence, no-handler operation).
- `@guardian/telemetry`: new error-shape contract tests.
- `bazelisk build //... && bazelisk test //...` green (91/91), typechecks clean.

## Summary

Fix the second PyPI publisher failure without changing CocoaPDF's package contents, conversion engine, native release pipeline, version policy, or Trusted Publishing boundary.

The hash-pinned `uv 0.12.0` wheel installed successfully, but the workflow compared `uv --version` against the exact string `uv 0.12.0`. In current uv, `--version` is equivalent to `uv self version` and includes build commit/date metadata; the documented `-V` form intentionally omits that suffix. The package installation therefore succeeded and only the overly strict diagnostic assertion failed.

- switch the publisher self-check from `uv --version` to the documented stable `uv -V` form;
- log the normalized installed publisher version before asserting the exact pin;
- add a focused regression test requiring `uv -V` and forbidding the previously failing exact `uv --version` assertion;

Beslutsunderlagets fjorton D-frågor, avgjorda av beställaren post för post. Underlaget är `KO-GRUPP-D-100-2026-08-19.md` i handoff-repot. Prövningskedjan kördes om över hela kön före godkännandena, så varje publicering gick genom kvalitetsfiltret.

**Kön 519 → 495. Aktiva löften 1 730 → 1 743.**

## Vad som avgjordes

| | Beslut | Utfall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **D1** | Breda uppräkningslöften utan egen nivå avvisas, delarna prissätts var för sig | 3 avvisade (95 000 mkr/år), 5 delposter publicerade |
| **D2** | Partiets egen nivå representerar, delarna grupperas | 3 publicerade, grupperade — sparar 18 000 mkr/år |
| **D4** | Faktasidan beskriver konstruktionen och representerar | 2 publicerade, grupperade |
| **D5** | Ett parti som upprepar sig har gjort ett löfte, inte två | 1 publicerat löfte tillbakadraget (−52 000 mkr) |
| **D6** | Posten med partiets båda egna priser behålls | 1 publicerad, 3 avvisade |
| **D7** | En underhållsskuld betas av — engångsbelopp, inte årlig nivå | 2 poster ombokförda |
| **D8** | Partiets egen siffra bär löftet, vår uppskattning grupperas under | 2 publicerade, grupperade |
| **D9** | Samma bemanning, samma belopp, en gång | 5 publicerade löften rättade |
| **D10** | Ett utfall i plånboken är inget prissatt åtagande | 1 500 mkr → 0, grupplänk borttagen |
| **D11** | Att fortsätta en ordning som redan gäller är ingen ny kostnad | 1 avvisad, 1 satt till 0 med nivån utskriven |
| **D12** | Perioden avgjord post för post ur citatet och källsidan | 7 poster, 1 publicerad |
| **D13** | Genomförd politik är inget löfte | 3 avvisade efter läsning |
| **D14** | En punkt under en viljebärande rubrik ärver den viljan | Regel fastställd |

## Tre fel som stod i publicerat data

**Ett lånat belopp följde inte med när originalet ändrades.** Socialdemokraternas bemanningslöfte gick 8 000 → 3 000 i juli och 3 000 → 1 950 i augusti när partiets egen siffra hittades. Liberalernas och Miljöpartiets löften om samma bemanning hade ankrat i mellansteget och stod kvar där. Och eftersom gruppen representeras av det högsta beloppet för mandatperioden bar Liberalernas föräldrade tal fortfarande **hela gruppens bidrag till rikssumman** — korrigeringen av partiets eget löfte hade alltså ingen effekt på summan.

**Samma 1,95 miljarder bokförda på två sätt i samma grupp** — ett löfte som årlig nivå, ett som engångsbelopp.

**Ett belopp byggt ur ett utfall.** «5 000 kronor i plånboken» delat på fyra år gånger ett antaget antal barnfamiljer gav 1 400 mkr — en statlig kostnad räknad ur ett utfall som partiets egna skattelöften redan är prissatta för.

Sex publicerade löften rättade med rättelsenot och egen historikpost på vart och ett.

## Två flaggor som pekade fel

**`belopp_avviker`: sex av sex falska larm.** Flaggan jämför beloppsfältet mot ett tal skrapat ur uträkningstexten, och det talet var uträkningens egen högsiffra, en delpost, eller i ett fall **100 GWh** — en volym, inte kronor. Tillämpad rakt av hade regeln «angivet belopp gäller» satt biogaslöftet till 100 miljoner och kärnkraftslöftet till 2 000 000. Ingen av de sex bar en partiangiven siffra.

**`genomford_politik`: fyra fel av sju.** Två pekade på politik som inte gäller i dag. Av de tre som höll, höll två på en annan grund — dåtid, «har föreslagit».

## Grindar

`pipeline` 675 prov, `handlingsvagen/pipeline` 314 prov, `site` hela sviten — alla gröna. `tsc --noEmit` rent. `data_hash` stämmer. Handlingsvågens läskopia och domar omgenererade; ett belägg flyttat och ett indraget efter indragningen, med rättelsenot — ingen partibedömning föll bort.

author: yarivluts
body:
Follow-up to #104, which merged before an independent adversarial review of the
diff finished (a concurrent scheduled run picked up and merged the PR while a
review agent was still auditing it — the same overlapping-run race this repo
has documented before, with KAN-20). The review found real issues in the
already-shipped audit coverage; fixing them here rather than losing the
findings.

## What was wrong

1. **A hardcoded `before` snapshot that a future guard change could seal as a
   lie.** `decideResourceAttachment` wrote `before: { status: 'pending' }` and
   `detachResource` wrote `before: { status: 'approved' }` as literals —
   true today only because of the guard immediately above each write.
   `recordAuditLogEntry`'s `entry_hash` commits over `before` in an
   append-only chain (`audit-log.service.ts`), so the moment either guard
   loosens (e.g. "let an org owner re-decide a rejected request"), the entry
   would cryptographically seal a value that was never true — and
   `verifyAuditLogChainForOrg` would still report the chain `valid: true`.
   Now both capture the actual prior value before mutating, the same pattern
   `setResourceAttachmentWriteTier` (same file) and `membership.service.ts`
   already use.

2. **snake_case fields in an otherwise all-camelCase convention.** The new
   `has_secret`/`resource_kind`/`resource_id` snapshot keys were the only new
   ones in this codebase to break the camelCase convention every one of the
   ~20 pre-existing `before`/`after` snapshots uses (`environmentId`,
   `fieldDefs`, `dailyQueryLimit`, `userId`, `boardIds`, ...) — including the
   identical "does this credential have a secret" concept, already
   `hasSecret` in `apps/web`'s own credentials route. Renaming this after the
   fact would mean either rewriting hash-committed historical entries or
   living with two conventions in the same collection forever, so fixing it
   now, before the first real entry accumulates.

3. **Attachment entries recorded *which* resource but not *what access*.**
   Missing `scopeSelection` — for a credential attachment, the scope
   selection *is* the grant (the codebase's own
   `listActiveAttachmentsForProject` doc comment calls it "the actual
   access-control read"). Added to all three attachment-lifecycle entries.

4. **Missing test coverage:**
   - a vault rotation attempted on a credential with no secret ever set now
     asserts it records nothing (the existing guard-failure pattern already
     used on the resource-attachment side)
   - the documented "`revealSharedCredentialSecret` is deliberately not
     audited" decision is now pinned by a test, not just a comment — so a
     future run "completing" the coverage doesn't quietly turn the audit log
     into a per-plugin-sync firehose
   - all three routes (`secret`, `secret/rotate`, `resource-attachments`)
     now assert the recorded `actor_id` is the *signed-in caller*, not some
     other id already in scope (e.g. a resource's own `created_by`/
     `requested_by`) — the one thing the route-level plumbing over the
     service layer actually establishes, previously asserted nowhere.

## Tests

`pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm test` (834 tests in
`firebase-orm-models`; `apps/web`'s vitest + Playwright suite green, one
unrelated pre-existing flaky e2e test — `schema-registry.spec.ts`, nothing to
do with this diff — passed on its automatic retry), and `pnpm build` all
green locally.

author: jrothrock
body:
## Why

Two things surfaced from a real Work-tab session (a worker verifying a PR inside a sandbox):

1. **A message typed into the Work tab was silently dropped.** The worker was mid-turn (stuck ~16 min in a `bundle`/`mise` loop), and the steer never appeared. Root cause: the WS reader did `select { case steerCh <- p: default: }`, and the run loop only *reads* the steer channel while parked idle **between** turns. A steer sent to a busy worker sat buffered with **zero feedback** — indistinguishable from "not sent" — and if the turn never ended, or 8+ piled up, it was lost.

2. **The worker skipped Docker-in-Docker** even though the sandbox had `DIND_ENABLED=1`. It installed Ruby via `mise` and pointed at host services instead of `docker compose up`. Not a sandbox failure — the conductor's worker prompt never encoded our "use DinD for services" convention.

## What

- **`mergeJob.queueSteer`** replaces the silent `select/default` send. It queues the prompt **and** gives visible feedback:
  - busy worker → *"💬 Message received — the worker is mid-step; it'll pick this up when the current step finishes."*
  - idle worker → applied immediately (the resulting turn is its own ack)
  - full buffer → an **error** line, never a silent drop
  - Shared by worker jobs **and** host-merge jobs (both attach via `attachMergeJobWS`).
- **Skill guidance** (`corral-api/SKILL.md`): a new "When a worker operates on a Corral project (sandbox)" section — run via `corral project exec`, **prefer DinD** for services (`DOCKER_HOST` is set; `docker compose up`/`docker run`; `dind-data/` volumes persist), **but fall back to installing requirements directly** when the app isn't containerized. Explicitly: getting the app runnable is the goal; DinD is the preferred means, not a hard requirement.

## Scope note

This makes steers **reliable and acknowledged**, not *interrupting*. True mid-turn interruption (killing/replacing the subprocess mid-run) is a larger, riskier change left as a possible follow-up.

## Tests

`TestQueueSteer` — idle (queued, silent), busy (queued + ack), full buffer (surfaced error), blank (ignored). Full `sqlite_fts5` build + `go vet` + `gofmt` green.

author: theagenticguy
body:
## Why

`claude-sql`'s effective freshness had decayed from hourly to **~2-hourly**, and a
file-watcher alone would not have fixed it. From `scripts/.run/claude-sql-refresh.log`
on the live host:

- Every hourly tick logged `skip: a refresh is already running`. Completions on
  2026-08-19: 00:29, 02:30, 04:36, 06:51, 08:29, 10:44, 12:57, 14:52, 16:39, 18:54,
  20:44 — **~2h apart**. On 08-18 they were ~1h apart, so the cadence decays as the
  corpus grows.
- One stage dominated: `UMAP 50d done in 414.0s`, `UMAP 2d done in 807.0s`,
  HDBSCAN 18.8s — **~21 minutes of full refit over 128,453 embeddings to absorb 14 new
  messages**.
- The 10:20Z LLM tick never ran that day: `10:20:02 skip: a refresh is already running`,
  and there is no `mode=--llm` completion for 08-19. The paid plane was starved by the
  free one sharing its `flock`.
- The skip gates were **inverted**. `cluster` keyed on an mtime sidecar so it rebuilt
  every tick (its input genuinely moved), while `terms` and `community` gated on bare
  parquet existence and were pinned at **2026-07-27** — c-TF-IDF labels describing a
  `cluster_id` partition that no longer existed, since HDBSCAN re-mints those ids on
  every fit.

## What this changes

**1. A connection can now say what instant it covers, and advance cheaply.**
`register_raw` records a per-file mtime watermark; `refresh_raw(con)` re-reads only the
files whose mtime moved; `snapshot_as_of(con)` reports coverage.

| operation | measured (9,082 files, live interactive corpus) |
|---|---|
| full `register_raw` | **6.2 s** |
| `refresh_raw`, one file changed | **0.22 s** |
| watermark bulk-insert vs `executemany` | 0.2 s vs **15.0 s** |

`snapshot_as_of` is the authoritative accessor `tower-bonk`'s
`claude_sql_store.py:35-41` names as blocked on this repo — it currently rebuilds its
whole connection on a timer and stamps its own clock instead.

**2. `claude-sql watch`** — a daemon that holds one connection and advances it as
transcripts land. OS events via `watchfiles` (new `watch` extra) with an mtime-polling
fallback behind one `FileWatcherPort`.

On the **hook-vs-file-watch** question: a `SessionEnd`-style hook is too late (an
interactive session stays open for hours and its rows should be queryable during it) and
not universal (it fires only where installed, while subagent sidecars, resumed sessions,
and any writer that does not load the hook config land as plain file writes). The
quiet-period debounce recovers the same "the turn finished writing" signal by observation
instead of announcement. The event stream decides *when* to refresh, never *what*: each
flush rescans the watermark, so a dropped inotify event self-heals.

Live smoke test on the real corpus:

```json
{"flush_index": 1, "files_touched_count": 2, "rows_inserted_count": 3218,
 "rows_deleted_count": 3211, "embedded_count": 0, "rebuilt": false,
 "covers_through": "2026-08-19T22:20:52.691272+00:00", "elapsed_seconds": 0.2}
```

Cost posture: the refresh is free; `--embed-limit` defaults to **0** (no provider calls
at all) and is a per-flush cap when enabled. There is deliberately no one-shot mode — a
fresh process has no prior snapshot to advance, so incrementality only pays inside a
resident process.

**3. `terms` and `community` now gate on their input's mtime**, via a single shared
`infrastructure/freshness.py` (also replacing `cluster`'s inline copy). The inputs differ
and that was part of the bug: `community` is Leiden+CPM over session centroids built
straight from `message_embeddings` and never reads `clusters.parquet`.

**4. The 2-D UMAP viz projection is opt-in** (`--viz` /
`CLAUDE_SQL_UMAP_COMPUTE_VIZ`). Nothing reads the `x`/`y` columns it fills —
`cluster_summary` uses `cluster_id` + `cluster_terms`, tower-bonk exposes no cluster
endpoint, and the console's one scatter is the sentiment arc. It was **807 s of a
1,247 s stage**. The columns stay in the schema holding NULLs.

## Verification

- `mise run check` green: lint + fmt + typecheck + import-linter + **847 tests** + proofs.
- `mise run security` — 40 findings, **all pre-existing** GitHub-workflow YAML
  (mutable action tags, dependabot cooldown). Zero in any Python file touched here.
- New Lean module `proofs/ClaudeSql/Debounce.lean` machine-checks the starvation guard:
  with `max_wait > 0` a file is due once `max_wait` has elapsed since its first event, for
  *any* amount of subsequent write activity. A pure quiet-period debounce lacks this and
  would never flush an actively-written session.
- Integration tier over real DuckDB + a real corpus, carrying the metarepo's standing
  lessons: one test seeds a **neighbour's** rows (a single-session corpus passes against
  an over-broad `DELETE`), one pins the delete-then-insert order (insert-only silently
  doubles a session's row count).
- **The three regression locks were verified to fail against the reintroduced bug**, not
  assumed to bite — the existence gate was patched back in and all three went red.

## Not in scope

The cron-side cadence fix (separate `flock` per plane so the nightly LLM run cannot be
eaten, embed on a short timer, clustering nightly) lives in the metarepo's
`scripts/claude-sql-refresh.sh` + crontab, not in this repo. Incremental UMAP
(`transform` on new points instead of `fit_transform` over the corpus) is the remaining
O(corpus) cost and is deliberately left for its own change — it alters cluster
assignment semantics and deserves separate validation.

author: pradeepkumar-qure
body:
## Problem

A `claude setup-token` credential is scoped to `user:inference` alone. The usage endpoint (`/api/oauth/usage`) needs profile scope, so these accounts 401/403 there on every pass and render a permanent `usage unavailable`.

The bigger consequence is invisibility to `cswap auto`: `_rank_candidates` skips any account whose headroom is `None`, so a setup-token account is never chosen as a switch target — and never triggers a switch away from itself, even at 100%.

```
2: user@example.com [personal]
   usage unavailable (http-403)
```

## Approach

Every `/v1/messages` response carries the same 5h/7d numbers in `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-*` headers, and inference is exactly what these tokens are permitted to do:

```
anthropic-ratelimit-unified-5h-utilization: 0.04
anthropic-ratelimit-unified-5h-reset: 1787184600
anthropic-ratelimit-unified-7d-utilization: 0.06
anthropic-ratelimit-unified-7d-reset: 1787655600
```

So for inference-only credentials, probe those headers instead of spending a guaranteed 401/403 per pass. The probe returns data in the *raw* usage-API shape, so `build_usage_result` normalizes it unchanged and nothing downstream needs to know the difference.

Detection is narrow — `scopes == {"user:inference"}` exactly — so full-scope logins keep using the real endpoint.

## Cost, and why it is throttled

The probe has to be a **successful** call. Rejected requests return no rate-limit headers at all; both were measured against the live API:

| request | status | rate-limit headers |
|---|---|---|
| empty `messages` array | 400 | none |
| bogus model name | 404 | none |
| minimal valid call | 200 | present |

So each probe costs one output token. `PROBE_MIN_INTERVAL_S` (default 600s, keyed by token digest) keeps the poll loop from consuming the very window it is measuring. Both the interval and the model are env-overridable (`CLAUDE_SWAP_PROBE_INTERVAL`, `CLAUDE_SWAP_PROBE_MODEL`) — a hardcoded model id eventually gets retired out from under us.

## Result

```
2: user@example.com [personal]
   ├ 5h:   3%   resets 16:00         in 31m
   └ 7d:  98%   resets Aug 22 05:00  in 2d 13h  (ahead of pace)
```

Verified against three real setup-token accounts, each reporting its own distinct utilization and reset times.

## Limitation

Per-model weekly windows are absent from the headers, so `--model` triggers stay blind for probed accounts. Account-wide 5h/7d — the windows that gate everything — now work.

## Tests

`tests/test_probe_usage.py`, 12 cases: scope detection, the 0-1 → 0-100 scaling (getting this wrong renders every percentage 100x low), epoch → ISO round trip through `format_reset`, normalization through `build_usage_result` into a non-`None` `account_headroom`, malformed/absent headers, and the throttle's cache-hit / expiry / per-token isolation.

Full suite: 2099 passed. One pre-existing failure (`test_settings.py::TestAtomicWriteThroughSymlink`) reproduces on a clean checkout of `main` — a WSL `/mnt/c` permissions quirk, unrelated to this change.

author: notasithlord
body:
## What changed

- Adds manifest-defined, code-first App actors bound to the exact App tab, root task, manifest revision, and caller authority.
- Adds a host-owned App-tab actor drawer whose messages enter the same durable bound-actor mailbox without an orchestrator proxy or sender-specific personality.
- Gives App actors a sealed `app_code` observe/act feedback loop while keeping runtime calls exact-instance, abort-aware, and outcome-safe.
- Adds deterministic, version-pinned compressed dwapp transport with compressed and decoded integrity commitments, bounded streaming decompression, compression-bomb rejection, exact compressed-chunk reseeding, and v1 reads.
- Keeps decoded source and binary assets readable in the OPFS/isomorphic-git working tree and exposes packaged assets through `peerd.assets`.
- Hardens App actor ownership, manifest reconciliation, runtime deadlines, and dweb bridge cancellation/epoch handling.

## Why

This makes distributed Apps first-class Peerd artifacts: an App can ship readable code and assets, run over the P2P network, and define a dedicated actor that can exercise and improve the App through a narrow semantic adapter. Charon is the initial end-to-end consumer, including multiplayer lobby coordination and actor-driven dogfooding.

## User and developer impact

- Users can import a `.peerd` App, open it from the Library, and message its dedicated actor directly from the App tab.
- App code can reveal the host drawer but cannot submit prompts, read the transcript, invoke providers, or obtain actor credentials/tools.
- App authors select a host-owned actor profile and provide subordinate manifest role context plus an optional bounded observe/act runtime.
- Seeders serve the exact signed compressed chunks, while installed repositories retain ordinary decoded files compatible with isomorphic-git.

## Validation

- `bun run test:functional:badge` — 6407/6407 passing
- focused App actor/message/prompt/host-security tests — 137/137 passing
- real Chrome in-browser suite — 944/944 passing
- `bun run typecheck`
- `bun run lint`
- `bun run check:docpaths`
- `bun run check:hygiene`
- `git diff --check`
- Charon full game/multiplayer/dwapp parity suite and Peerd import compatibility passed against this integration tree

author: adamawan
body:
Rarity was carried by the egg and by however much marking a grid happened to have, and by nothing else — so a well-drawn common out-dressed a dull rare, which is exactly what it looked like. `berth` (common) read as a boat with a hull; `ingot` (rare) read as a lozenge with a stripe.

Two independent changes, both in `web/src/pets/`.

## The rim light

A pass over every grid, not a redraw. Each body pixel scores its four neighbours: open to the top-left takes the highlight, open to the bottom-right takes a new `shade` ink. The hand-placed `h` dots fold back into the body first, so a grid is lit once rather than lit *and* blushed.

It rounds all 81 grids without touching one of them, and keeps working — a grid changed tomorrow is lit for free. Memoised against the grid's identity, which holds because every caller passes a module constant out of `spriteFor`. Across the set it touches ~38% of body pixels: least on the slim ones (`nib`, `quill`, `pip`), most on the broad flat ones (`cairn`, `bramble`, `vellum`), which is where the drawing was emptiest.

## The rarity ladder

`dressSprite` holds it whole: one grid in, one dressed grid out. Each tier keeps everything below it and adds one device it is not allowed.

| Tier | Adds |
| --- | --- |
| `common` | the lit body, and nothing else |
| `uncommon` | one appendage above the head, drawn in its own grid |
| `rare` | an angular silhouette, and four glints just outside its bounding box |
| `mythic` | a glow past the outline, and a sparkle that moves |

`cairn`, `ingot`, `lander` and `quill` are redrawn angular, and nothing below them is. That is the load-bearing half of the rare rung: the shape says the tier at 24px in the enclosure, where four glints are four pixels.

## Notes for a reviewer

**The sparkle takes a phase, never a clock.** `dressSprite(grid, rarity, seed, phase)` stays pure, so a reload, a re-render or two surfaces showing one pet all draw the same star — the same property the crack overlay has by being indexed on rocks, and for the same reason. `PetSprite.useTwinkle` advances the phase off `beatMs`, the clock the idle bob already runs on, so a busy fleet twinkles faster and a paused one holds still at no second timer. It is never even started for the twenty species with nothing to twinkle, and `prefers-reduced-motion` holds phase 0 — the glow and a spark or two stay lit, so the tier's device survives even when its motion does not.

**Padding is constant at every tier.** A margin that varied by rarity would make the drawn size vary by rarity, and a rare would sit a pixel lower in the enclosure than the common beside it for no reason a reader could name. `SpeciesSprite` therefore takes its scale from the *undressed* grid — sizing from the dressed one shrinks every creature by a fifth to make room for the margin — and offsets the crack overlay by `SPRITE_PAD`.

**Two calls made while building.** Unopened mythics twinkle too: the shell is banded end to end precisely to say the tier, so holding the sparkle back would withhold nothing and cost the moment it is most worth having. And the rare's glints sit just *outside* the bounding box corners rather than on it — on the box, the two flank glints landed on the widest part of the animal and silently vanished, so four glints were two.

**The withheld state gets louder.** An unfound rare still glints and an unfound mythic still glows on the Pets page. That follows the page's existing split — identity is withheld, price is published, and a tier is price — but it is a change to what withholding says, and it is written down in the spec.

## Verification

`npm run check` passes all six stages. `test/petSprites.test.ts` covers the properties that break quietly: every emitted character has an ink, padding is exact at every tier and stage, the ladder never runs downhill, a mythic is never dark and never fires all four sparks at once, and one phase always draws one sparkle.

Checked in the running cockpit: sprites render, the mythic egg's canvas changes between samples while the three non-mythics stay byte-identical (so no wasted redraws), no console errors, no layout overflow in the enclosure.

Two things I could not check. The Pets **catalogue** page does not render in demo mode ("built from the harness's own tables, which this build does not run"), so the withheld path — where devices draw in a fainter grey than the silhouette — is untested by eye. Separately, the canvases show antialiased edges from a fractional device-pixel ratio; that is pre-existing rather than from this change, but it does undercut the draw loop's "whole pixels only" rule and may be worth its own look.

Spec updated in the same change: `docs/spec/22-pets.md#the-rarity-ladder` now owns the ladder, why the sparkle takes a phase, and what the ladder does to the withheld state.

author: joseustra
body:
Adds `claude/skills/orchestrator/SKILL.md` — a Claude session the human talks to, which delegates all work and performs none of it.

Six commits, one new file. The later five are amendments and three rounds of self-review; the reviews are on disk at `/tmp/orchestrator-selfreview{,-2,-3}.md`.

## What the skill defines

- **The four command families** it may run — `grove`, `helm-cli`, `gh` reads plus issue comments, `git` reads — and a "what this will not do" section written as refusals rather than advice.
- **Dispatch**: write the brief, check the trunk, then `grove new` → `helm-cli warm` → `sleep 4` → one `helm-cli prompt` carrying `claude "read /tmp/brief-<ticket>.md and do exactly what it says"`.
- **Status with two speeds**: facts now from `grove list`, `helm-cli ls --json`, `git` and `gh`; a worker's own answer later or never. Answer from facts first, never narrate what a worker is doing, never go quiet waiting.
- **Fixed output shapes** for DISPATCH, STATUS, RELAY and RETIRE, with every column bound to the command that produces it.
- **No ledger.** The ticket is the join key; grove holds the mapping.

## Design decisions worth reviewing

**One orchestrator serves one repository.** `grove new` runs in the working directory and takes no path. Scoping to one repo means the orchestrator never needs `cd`, which the four command families never allowed. A second repo gets a second orchestrator.

**Sessions are discardable.** Helm closing or the Mac rebooting means starting again. The skill does not engineer around durability: briefs live in `/tmp`, and a brief that is gone is written again from the issue.

**No dispatch verification.** An earlier commit added a `ps` check that the exact line landed. It could not work — `ps -ax -o args= | grep -F <line>` matches the wrapper shell holding the pipeline in its argv, and the grep itself, so it reported "landed" with nothing dispatched. It was removed rather than repaired. The skill now reports what it sent, never what arrived, and says a corrupted dispatch surfaces as no reply, no commits and no PR.

**A worker reply needs no protocol.** It arrives in the orchestrator pane, prefixed with the worker's address so it can be told apart from the human. That prefix is obligatory in the brief footer.

## Verified rather than asserted

Each of these was run on this machine, not reasoned about:

- every fish block parses under `fish -n`;
- `set p (cmd)` propagates `$status` — the launcher's no-project branch is real, `helm-cli current --project` exits 1 here;
- `{owner}`/`{repo}` survive fish unexpanded (fish expands a brace list only when it holds a comma), so `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/...` is safe;
- the trunk check prints `on feat/orchestrator-skill, not main` from this branch;
- `grove list` shows ticket `254-ctrl-c-freeze` on branch `joseustra/254-ctrl-c-freeze` — the branch is not the ticket, so the skill reads the `BRANCH` column;
- grove's `STATUS` column says `running` while no `claude` process exists, so it is not worker liveness;
- Claude Code's Read tool does resolve a `~` path, so the tilde in the dispatched line is fine.

One claim in the file is explicitly *not* verified, and says so: nothing has restarted Helm to confirm panes die with it. It no longer carries weight, since the restart path is "start again" either way.

## One note for the reviewer

**The published `helm-cli` skill is out of date.** `~/.claude/skills/helm-cli/SKILL.md` documents only `new`/`ls`/`rm`/`projects`/`current`. The binary at `~/.local/bin/helm-cli` also has `prompt`, `warm`, `--label` on `new`, and `--address` on `current` — all of which this skill depends on. Flags and exit codes here come from `helm-cli help`, which is the newer source. That skill file wants updating separately.

```
Received string:  "text/html"
```

**200, not 404.** Every unmatched path falls through to the SPA, so the missing icon returns a perfectly successful HTML response. A check asserting only the status code passes over this bug — that's exactly how the first version of this test in web-template#92 passed against the very defect it was written for. The content type is what distinguishes *served* from *swallowed*.

After the fix, verified the way the bug demands — the **built** output, not the dev server:

```
dist/index.html:  rel="icon" ... href="/snipit/balenthiran.svg"
dist/balenthiran.svg          <- present in the dist root
```

Declared **and** served. Vite rewrites the root-absolute href against `base` at build time, which is why `/balenthiran.svg` in source is correct here.

</details>

<details>
<summary>The decoy that hid this, and why it is deleted rather than moved</summary>

`frontend/src/public/logo.svg` was **byte-identical** to the real icon (same md5, `4680207...`) but sat in a directory Vite never publishes — `publicDir` is `frontend/public`. Present in the repo, absent from the site, referenced by nothing.

That is what made this invisible: grep for `logo.svg` and a file comes back, so the declaration looks satisfied. The same decoy hid the same bug in holiday-planning for the entire life of its deployment. Deleted rather than relocated — `public/balenthiran.svg` already serves it.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Suite</summary>

`tools/verify.js`: **66 dotnet / 65 unit / 7 e2e / lint 0**.

e2e went 6 -> 7: the new guard is *added*, not displacing an existing spec. The `openapi.json` drift this build produces is the known environmental noise (ordinal vs case-insensitive comparer) — reverted, not committed.

Ported the guard from web-template#92 rather than writing a new one, so the template and its apps fail the same way for the same reason.

</details>

author: wolf-achtung
body:
## Was passiert ist

Nach dem Merge von #366 fiel auf `main` ein Backend-Test:

```
FAILED test_wartung_2026_08_20.py::test_die_pruefliste_verliert_nichts
AssertionError: Die openReview-Zählung ist verschwunden oder umbenannt.
```

Der Lint-Durchgang hatte die tote Variable `openReview` aus `AdminApp.jsx` entfernt — und dieser Test hing daran.

**Der Test hatte recht damit, dass er fiel. Aber aus dem falschen Grund.**

## Der eigentliche Fehler ist älter

`test_die_pruefliste_verliert_nichts` stammt aus #363 und sollte die Zusage von Fund C absichern: ein Asset, dessen LLM-Antwort leer blieb, bekommt `needs_review` statt `new` — und muss dem Admin trotzdem vor Augen kommen. Umetikettieren darf nichts verstecken.

Nachgesehen hat der Test in dieser Zeile:

```js
const openReview = assets.filter((a) => a.review_status === 'new' || a.review_status === 'needs_review').length;
```

Die Zeile wurde **nie gerendert**. Sie ist beim Aufteilen der alten Admin-Datei in `AdminApp.jsx` mitgewandert, die Kopfzeile, die sie anzeigte, nicht. Der Test meldete also Sicherheit über etwas, das er nie geprüft hat: die Zusage lautete „der Admin sieht `needs_review`-Assets", nachgesehen wurde in einer Zeile, die kein Nutzer je zu Gesicht bekam.

Das ist schlimmer als kein Test. Ein fehlender Test ist eine bekannte Lücke; dieser hier war eine unbekannte.

Aufgefallen ist es nur, weil die Löschung ihn zum Fallen brachte. Hätte #366 die Variable stehenlassen, wäre der blinde Fleck geblieben — und ich hätte in #366 fälschlich behauptet, die Löschung sei folgenlos.

## Was jetzt geprüft wird

Die drei Stellen, die tatsächlich darüber entscheiden, ob ein `needs_review`-Asset sichtbar ist:

| # | Datei | Zusage |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `AdminApp.jsx` | Der Default-Status-Filter steht auf `'all'` — `visibleAssets` filtert nur, wenn er das *nicht* tut |
| 2 | `ReviewPanel.jsx` | `needs_review` steht in `STATUS_OPTIONS`, ist also gezielt auswählbar |
| 3 | `AssetCard.jsx` | Der Status hat eine Beschriftung („Noch zu prüfen") und wird nicht roh oder leer gerendert |

**Drei Mutationen verifiziert** — jede lässt den Test fallen:

| Mutation | |
|---|---|
| `status: 'all'` → `status: 'new'` | ✅ fällt |
| `needs_review` aus `STATUS_OPTIONS` entfernt | ✅ fällt |
| `needs_review:`-Beschriftung aus `AssetCard` entfernt | ✅ fällt |

Die Löschung in #366 war richtig und bleibt. **1565 Tests grün.**

## Nebenbefund: CI konnte das nicht sehen

`backend-tests.yml` läuft mit einem Pfad-Filter auf `backend/**`. Die CI von #366 hat den Fehler deshalb nicht bemerkt — eine reine Frontend-Änderung kann einen Backend-Test brechen, weil einige Wartungs-Tests absichtlich über die Grenze lesen (genau das ist ihr Zweck: eine Zusage prüfen, die beide Seiten betrifft).

Ich habe den Filter **nicht** geändert. Er spart bei jedem Frontend-PR zwei Minuten Postgres-Hochfahren, und es sind heute nur zwei Tests, die hinüberlesen. Aber die Lücke gehört benannt: wenn du willst, ziehe ich `frontend/**` als zusätzlichen Trigger nach — oder die grenzüberschreitenden Tests wandern in einen eigenen, schnellen Job ohne Datenbank. Sag, was dir lieber ist.

author: thales-da-vinci
adamlewis73
body:
The last piece of Phase 2's stated goal. Typing `先生と生産` segments into **先生 / と / 生産** as chips; tapping one shows its entry.

Confirmed on a device: tapping 生産 gives せいさん *"production; manufacture"* with **生** *life, genuine* and **産** *products, bear* beneath. The same 生 that means "life" on its own, sitting inside a word meaning "production" — the contextual point the app exists to make, now demonstrable end to end.

## Where it lives, and why

`KuromojiTokenizer` implements the domain `Tokenizer` interface and lives in `:data`, **not** `:domain`. Kuromoji is a plain JVM library, so `:domain` would compile — but it is JVM-**only** and cannot run on iOS, so putting it there would quietly undo exactly what D-60 protects. D-08 put the interface in the domain layer for this reason: replacing it later is one class, not a rewrite.

Seven unit tests cover it and run **on the JVM in milliseconds**, despite living in an Android module, because Kuromoji needs no device.

## Three details that would otherwise be silent wrong answers

- **Kuromoji writes the literal string `*`** for fields it has no value for. Passed through, that becomes a lookup for `"*"` — which returns nothing and reads as a missing dictionary entry rather than a bug.
- **Inflected words fall back to the base form**, so a sign reading 生きた finds 生きる. Without it the app says "not in the dictionary", which is wrong *and* looks like missing data rather than a missing lookup.
- **Particles stay in the token list.** Dropping them would corrupt every offset after them — and those offsets are what the scan overlay will use to map a tap back to a word (`architecture.md` stage 4, V-11). They're marked instead, so the UI can show them muted without offering "case marking particle" as something to learn.

Tokenization runs on `Dispatchers.Default`; Kuromoji reads a ~12 MB IPADIC dictionary from its jar on first use.

## Cost

**APK grows 52 MB → 64 MB**, almost entirely that dictionary.

## Licensing, which the build tried to make easy to get wrong

Kuromoji is Apache 2.0 — a third category of obligation after the CC BY-SA datasets and the OFL font — and its two jars ship identical `META-INF` licence files. The build fails with:

```
2 files found with path 'META-INF/LICENSE.md'
```

That reads like a packaging annoyance, and the obvious fix (`excludes`) would silently drop the licence from the APK. It uses `pickFirsts` instead, keeping one copy. Verified `META-INF/LICENSE.md` and `NOTICE.md` are present in the built APK, and `attribution.md` now covers Kuromoji explicitly.

## Verified

7 instrumented tests, 7 tokenizer unit tests, 10/10 verification cases, 38 dictbuild unit tests, `:domain:test`.

## Still open

- **No UI tests.** The ViewModel's stale-result guard — each keystroke cancels the previous lookup — remains untested.
- **D-07's longest-match alternates** aren't implemented; Kuromoji's segmentation is taken as-is. `roadmap.md` parks ambiguity chips deliberately, so this is the recorded position rather than an omission.

author: adamtheturtle
body:
Two of the High-severity Cursor Bugbot comments left unresolved on merged pull requests.

- **`super()` no longer resolves to the class the call is written in** (#368). Zero-argument `super()` was resolved as the enclosing class, the same starting point as `self`. Python skips that class in the MRO, so when a subclass also defines the method and `--fix` removed a default from it, the subclass's default was written into the call instead of the parent's — changing what the call does. Lookup now starts at the bases.
- **A system-owned extended attribute no longer aborts the whole run** (#193). `copy_extended_attributes` treated any failed `set_xattr` as fatal. macOS keeps names such as `com.apple.macl` and `com.apple.provenance` on ordinary files and refuses to let a user process write them, so a project containing one file with such an attribute was left entirely unfixed. Those are skipped; every attribute that can be copied still is.

Six further comments in that batch — the protocol-allowlist ones on #455, #456, #457, #459, #461 and #466 — were closed by the later `Retain … protocol defaults` pull requests, which extended the allowlist to every dunder they named. Those threads are resolved without a code change here.

## Validation

- `cargo test --locked` (304 tests)
- `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo fmt --check`

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes how `--fix` rewrites `super()` calls (behavioral correctness) and atomic file replacement on macOS; both are localized but affect real fix output.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`super().method()` fixes now follow Python’s MRO.** Zero-argument `super()` was resolved like `self`, so when a subclass overrides a method, `--fix` could inject the subclass’s removed default into `super().target()` instead of the parent’s. Lookup now starts at base classes via `super_method`, with `receiving_class` tracking a `through_super` path so attribute calls use the right signature.
> 
> **macOS fix runs no longer abort on system xattrs.** While copying extended attributes onto fixed files, any `set_xattr` failure was fatal. Apple-owned attributes (`com.apple.macl`, `com.apple.provenance`, etc.) return permission denied; those are skipped on macOS so the rest of the project can still be fixed. Writable attributes are still copied as before.

author: cpheinrich
body:
A review could be merged past unread, or outrun mid-flight. Reading the branch protection made it
worse than the question implied: **Morpheus's `main` required zero status checks** — a PR could
merge with CI red or still running — which is also what let `--auto` once merge a stale head
(`learned.md` records the bite). Evo requires `web` and `pm` only. Neither repo requires
conversation resolution.

The settled decision — *rung 2 does not block* — stands. It forbids the review's **verdict** gating
the merge; this PR gates the **process**: the review must have finished, and every finding must be
visibly dispositioned. The reviewer can insist on being read; it still cannot stop a merge by being
wrong.

**What changed**

- **`agent-review / delivery` fails** on a requested, configured, undelivered review, where it used
  to warn and pass — green-with-warning is a gate that never closes. Because it `needs: review`, an
  in-flight review holds it *pending*, which is what actually stops `--auto` and manual merges
  mid-review once the check is required. Legitimate skips (records-only PRs, unconfigured repos,
  `synchronize` pushes) leave the job skipped, which satisfies a required check.
- **`review-waived: <reason>`** in the PR body is the pressure valve — requiring delivery without
  it would have turned the six-day credit outage into six days of blocked merges. Reuses
  `waiverReason` + `isRealReason` from `check pr` (one definition, third consumer), validated the
  same way (`review-waived: yes` is refused), reported on the check rather than swallowed, read at
  verification time so the recovery is edit-body-and-re-run. **A waiver never relabels an actual
  delivery**, and an unreadable PR body is no waiver — fail closed.
- **`review delivery` grows `--pr-body-file`**; the workflow fetches the body and passes it.
- **Docs**: architecture §9 records the enforcement design and its one accepted seam (a push made
  during the previous commit's in-flight review can outrun it — closing that window costs per-push
  reviews, the bill already declined); AGENTS.md gets the disposition loop — wait for delivery,
  read findings, reply where declining, resolve every thread, never `--admin`.
- Also carries the §9 credential paragraph written for #133 and missed by that commit's `git add`.

**After this merges** (settings, not files — applied by hand and recorded in §9): required checks
on Morpheus `node / check`, `pm / pm`, `pr / conventions`, `agent-review / delivery`; on Evo the
existing two plus `agent-review / delivery`; conversation resolution required on both.

## Test plan

`pnpm typecheck && pnpm test && pnpm compile && pnpm morpheus pm index` clean — 931 tests, 7 new.

- Five on `reviewDelivery`: a real waiver passes and is labelled `waived:`; `review-waived: yes`
  is refused; no waiver fails; a missing PR-body file is no waiver; a waiver never relabels an
  actual delivery.
- Two workflow guards, one verified by breaking its subject: softening the delivery step's final
  `exit 1` back to a warning fails `fails on a non-delivery, and honours a spoken waiver`.

**The live proof is this PR itself**: its review runs under the new delivery step, delivery must
pass as a check that is now capable of failing, and once conversation resolution is flipped on, any
inline finding on this PR physically blocks the merge until resolved.

## Open questions

None. The one judgment call — waivable rather than hard-blocking when the reviewer is down — was
made by Chris in chat, and the waiver's visibility is what keeps it honest.

author: sarahrosehassan
body:
Closes #69. Closes #70.

Both from Dave at the Aug 19 meeting.

## Furthest behind first (#69)

> the list of people to mark will be prioritized by the person who's the furthest behind... just in case we run out of time in a given session

The queue was first-come-first-served. That is a fairness rule of its own, and this **replaces** it with a different one: when a session runs out of time, the people who miss out should be the ones who can most afford to. Worth being explicit that a student who is ahead may now wait longer, or not be seen at all in a busy session. That is the intent.

**Percentage, not a raw count.** A part-time student has 40 competencies and a full-time one has 80, so counting raw would park every part-time student at the top of the queue for the entire term. There's a test for that.

**Tie-break is `requested_at`**, so students on the same completion keep first-come-first-served between them. Done with a stable sort over the existing query order rather than more SQL.

## Catching up after a missed week (#70)

> an ACR can cover three days... those three that they would have missed, three, so nine evaluations they would have missed, will kind of move forward to the following week

The three-per-session cap is a **spreading** rule, not a rationing one: it stops someone doing forty in one sitting. A student who was ill did not choose to bunch their work, so the cap was punishing them for something it was never aimed at.

Their cap is now raised by one session's worth for each session missed in the previous week, giving Dave's 3 + 9 = 12.

**Two deliberate limits:**

- **Bounded to one week.** Missing a month does not entitle anyone to a 39-competency session.
- **It expires.** A rolling window, not a bank. Dave's framing is catching up *the following week*, and a balance that accumulated all term would undo the spreading rule entirely.

**The student is told why**, or a cap that silently reads 12 looks like a bug rather than a kindness.

**The balance rule still applies** at the higher cap, so catching up does not become bingeing one course.

## Open question for Dave, in #70

Should this apply to any missed session, or only an excused one? His example is an ACR, but the app has no notion of an excused absence and adding one is a much bigger change. Built the generous version: any missed session counts, nobody has to administer absence notes, and the worst case is a student who skipped a week being allowed to catch up, which is the outcome we want anyway.

## Notes

- 208 tests pass, 11 new.

author: steffen74
body:
## Why

Documentation instructions were an admin-only catalogue. An instructor who
wanted a write-up guide tailored to their own course had to ask an admin. This
adds an upload dialog next to **all three** instruction dropdowns (the
management grid's expanded row, **Add project**, **Confirm team**) where an
instructor can create an instruction for the current project type — and rename,
replace the PDF of, or delete the ones they created.

## Ownership model

New nullable `ProjectDocumentationInstruction.createdByUserId`:

- **NULL — platform instruction.** Admin-maintained, visible to every
  instructor. Every pre-existing row is NULL, so nothing changes for anyone
  today.
- **Set — personal instruction.** Only its creator may rename it, replace its
  PDF, or delete it. Stamped by a Hasura **insert preset**, never sent by the
  client, so ownership cannot be forged.

Instructor select is `platform OR own OR isDefault OR attached-to-a-project-I-teach-or-mentor`.
The last two clauses are correctness, not convenience: without `isDefault` a
promoted default becomes invisible and `handleSetProjectType` starts refusing
type changes; without the project clause the *mutation-driven* dropdown renders
a value outside its own options and a co-instructor can silently reassign it.
Students and anonymous keep unfiltered select so a team can always open the
instruction its project points at.

Only platform instructions can become a type default. Titles are unique per
owner, and globally unique among platform rows (a global constraint would reject
a title whose owner the caller cannot even see, and leak its existence).

## Security fixes this widening made necessary

**The main one:** `saveProjectDocumentationInstruction` derives the storage
object key from the instruction id supplied by the caller, and the generic
`saveFile` handler never checked ownership. Granting the action to instructors
as-is would have let one instructor **overwrite another instruction's PDF** —
including admin-uploaded files that students download — since the stored `url`
reveals the exact target path. A file-type allowlist does not help: the upload
is a valid PDF, just aimed at someone else's object. A dedicated handler now
verifies ownership before delegating to `saveFile`.

The seven migration-seeded defaults point at static Next.js paths and were never
reachable this way; every GCS-backed upload was.

Also in scope because they became reachable:

- **No file validation at all.** The action set no `allowed-file-extensions`, so
  `saveFile` skipped `validateFileUpload` entirely. Now `.pdf` enforced by magic
  bytes (`%PDF-` + trailing `%%EOF`), with the previously-implicit 20 MiB cap
  pinned explicitly.
- **Unsanitised `filename` in the object key.** `replacePlaceholders` substitutes
  it verbatim. Production GCS does not resolve `..`, but the emulated dev bucket
  writes through `fs`, where the OS does — an arbitrary file write. Fixed
  centrally in `saveFile` *and* `saveImage`, so it also closes the pre-existing,
  already-reachable path via `saveProjectDocumentation`.
- **Instructor-writable `url`** could point an instruction at any public object
  in the bucket → check constraint pinning owned rows to the action's prefix.
- **Promoting a personal instruction to a type default** is refused.

### Bug found along the way

`saveFile`'s failure branches omitted `filePath`/`accessUrl`, which
`saveFileResult` declares non-null. Hasura discarded the entire payload with
`expecting not null value for field "filePath"`, so `FILE_TOO_LARGE` and
`INVALID_FORMAT` never reached the client as readable messages — for any
`saveFile` action, not just this one. Fixed by returning empty strings; callers
branch on `success` first.

## Review notes

- The grid's instruction block previously rendered only when the option list was
  non-empty, which would have made the new button unreachable for a type with no
  instruction yet. The condition is widened and the dropdown itself is guarded.
- `ConfirmProjectDialog`'s seeding effect depends on the instruction list's
  identity, which the post-create refetch changes — it would have overwritten the
  freshly created selection with the type default. Now guarded per opened project.
- `FileUploadField` was **not** reused for the replace control: it always renders
  a remove button which, without a `removeMutation`, falls back to the update
  mutation and writes `url = NULL` — hiding an instruction that projects still
  reference. An explicit replace control shares the create flow's upload routine
  instead.
- `ON DELETE RESTRICT` on the new FK, not `SET NULL`: user removal here is
  anonymisation (the `User` row survives), and `SET NULL` would silently promote a
  departed instructor's private instruction to platform-wide.
- Creating from this dialog **as a super-admin** produces a platform row (no
  preset for `admin`), which is the correct admin semantic but means it will not
  appear in the dialog's "your instructions" list. Documented as intended.

## Verification

Backend contract exercised directly against Hasura with real `instructor` /
`user` / `anonymous` roles:

- insert cannot set `createdByUserId` or `isDefault` (absent from the input type)
- instructor B cannot see, update or delete instructor A's row; still sees all
  platform rows; a student **can** read A's row; anonymous cannot
- `url` outside the allowed prefix → check-constraint violation
- raw delete of a row that has a PDF → zero rows (must go through the action)
- **action with a foreign instruction id → `..._UNAUTHORIZED`, bucket object
  untouched**; platform id → same
- `../../../evil.pdf` → stored inside `instruction-<id>/`, verified on the dev
  container filesystem
- a zip renamed `.pdf` → `INVALID_FORMAT`
- delete action: non-owner → `..._FORBIDDEN`, default → `..._IS_DEFAULT`,
  owner → succeeds; `setProjectDocumentationInstructionDefault` on a personal row
  → `..._NOT_PLATFORM`

Browser (Playwright, logged in as a real instructor): create → auto-selected in
the dropdown and persisted → listed for management → rename → replace PDF →
delete, all against the running stack. Test data cleaned up afterwards.

Migration applies, rolls back (restoring the global title constraint) and
re-applies. `yarn tsc --noEmit` clean, `yarn lint` clean apart from one
pre-existing warning in `TableGrid/hooks.ts`, frontend 127/127, functions 116/116
plus 30 new tests. `matrixRoomUtils.test.js` fails on a clean tree too (it uses
`node:test`, so Jest sees no tests in it) — pre-existing and unrelated.

Docs: new §7.3a and an ownership section in `PROJECTS_USER_MANUAL.md`, plus a
§8.1 isolation matrix and negative-GraphQL checklist in
`PROJECTS_TESTING_GUIDE.md`. The stale claim that delete is unavailable for
referenced rows is corrected — the action reassigns them.

author: gattia
body:
## What Phase 2 is

The documentation-accuracy pass. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` counts **31 public symbols whose docstrings contradict the code** — but that count came from reading, against a commit where `sdf_dataset.py` has since moved 100+ lines. Each has to be re-verified rather than trusted, so this does not try to close all 31 at once.

**This PR does the slice a machine can decide**: a name in an `Args:` block that is not in the signature. Only three functions had one, and two were live defects rather than typos.

## The two real ones

**`read_mesh_get_sampled_pts`** documented `return_orig_mesh`, `return_new_mesh` and `return_orig_pts` as parameters *"Defaults to False"*. The body lists all three as deprecated and prints *"always True"* — the opposite of what the docstring promised. Removed from `Args:`, and the deprecation list now records what the prose used to claim so the next reader doesn't reinstate it.

**NSM's own call site was still passing two of them**, so every mesh load printed a deprecation line nobody could act on:

```
return_orig_mesh is deprecated and not used in this function - always True
```

Removed. They were ignored, so nothing changes but the noise.

**`compute_recon_loss`** documented `orig_pts`, which is commented out of its signature, and omitted `orig_meshes` — the parameter that replaced it — plus `n_samples_assd` and `calc_assd`.

The third hit was a false positive: `triplanar.forward`'s `Note:` section parsed as a parameter name. The checker now knows the Google-style section headings.

## Keeping it fixed

`testing/NSM/test_docstring_signatures.py` asserts every documented parameter exists.

**The inverse check is deliberately absent.** Plenty of functions here document only the interesting arguments, and failing on that would be noise rather than signal — so an undocumented parameter is not an error.

Verified it fails as intended by reinstating `orig_pts` and watching it name the function and the phantom parameter.

## A bug in my own test, worth recording

Both doc tests now read with `encoding="utf-8"` explicitly. **Something else in the suite resets the locale to ASCII**: a bare `read_text()` passes in isolation and raises `UnicodeDecodeError` on the first non-ASCII character once the full suite runs. It cost 27 failures to find, and the reason is now a comment in the file so nobody simplifies it back.

## What Phase 2 still has left

The remaining contradictions are **semantic** — the prose describes behaviour the body does not have — and no test can see those. They need reading, module by module, and `docs/AUDIT_FINDINGS.md` has leads but its own banner says most entries were never executed and were written against an older commit. The concentration is `sdf_dataset.py` (7), `refine_mesh.py` (6), `reconstruct/main.py` (5), `mesh/main.py` (5).

## Verification

`353 passed, 1 skipped, 18 xfailed`. `make lint` passes.

author: angelcreator113
body:
Adds one index artifact. **Not a revision, not a specification, not an authorization. Mints nothing, closes nothing, picks no disputed value, changes no gate.**

**Why this exists.** v2.54 landed at `8a537c9c` and owes v2.55 several items. That list was reconstructible only by reading v2.54 §4/§5/§6 alongside FD-66 §5.1 and the commit log. **This puts it in a container.** Every entry cites a landed source — a v2.54 section, an FD-66 section or banner, or a commit SHA. No entry is sourced to a session transcript, which is what makes it writable without a cold read: it is transcription, not judgment.

**Five owed items, with the distinction that matters preserved.** Work-done-record-owed (the before/after pair — migration `956697c0`, test `16c47a5f`) is separated from not-started (F-Auth-5 closure, v2.54 §5). FD-66 §5.1's clause 3 closure record and v2.54 §5's still-owed infrastructure read at FD-66 §6.4.1 are listed with their sources.

**§1 item 3 — the `down` verification gate, and the sharpest entry.** v2.54 §1.2 calls this migration precedent-setting, being the first schema change under the FD-66 §7.1 migrations-only ruling. §2 step 2b is a gate whose stated consequence is that the migration does not ship if `down` fails. **The migration shipped at `956697c0` and no landed commit records the gate being exercised.** Two readings fit and an index cannot separate them: 2b ran unrecorded, or 2b did not run. **If the latter, the precedent set is not the one v2.54 intended.** Stated as absence of evidence, not as a claim the gate was skipped. Partly re-derivable — the `down` is still in the migration file — but **a green result does not close the item**: green tests the artifact and leaves the process question exactly where it was, while red would prove the gate had something to catch. Only a record of 2b having been exercised discharges it.

**§3 — a v2.54 citation that is already superseded.** v2.54 §6 states *"Axis P at FD-66 §6.3.1 has 19 members."* FD-66's own CORRECTION BANNER B1, added after `79f9bab1`, supersedes it with three figures on different bases: **19** (as filed, wrong method), **13** (corrected, same commit `77fc5fb0`), **12** (corrected, `main` at 2026-08-18, `decision_logs` having left the set via `956697c0` — v2.54's own migration). **The method was wrong, not only the count**: `Model.options.paranoid` was the exposure test, but a model with `timestamps: false` resolves no deletion attribute at all. **All three are recorded with their bases and none is picked** — picking is the cold read.

**§3.1 — the generalization, and the reason §3 is not a complaint about FD-66.** FD-66 §6.3.1's body still reads `Axis P (19)` because additive-supersede prepends banners and never rewrites bodies. **That is the convention working as designed** — a rewritten body destroys the record of what was believed and when. The cost is structural and not specific to FD-66: **every banner-carrying document holds superseded text that still reads as authoritative**, and any pointer aimed at a section rather than the document lands on it. v2.54 §6 was correct when written; §6.3.1 acquired a governing banner afterwards. No error at either end — the citation went stale by mechanism. **Rule recorded: a pointer into a banner-carrying document must resolve to the banner first**; the resolvable form is *"document §N, as corrected by banner B"*. Register-level observation, explicitly not a ruling — whether banners should enumerate the body sections they govern is left open.

**What it does not establish.** Not that the list is complete — an obligation recorded nowhere but a transcript is not here. Not that any owed item is still correct to do. Not the value of any disputed figure.

Docs only, one new file, 175 lines. No measurement performed. No FD minted, closed, or reprioritized. No schema or deployed host contacted. Prod FROZEN.

body:
## Summary
Closes #1558. `request_body_size_middleware` only inspected `Content-Length`, so HTTP/1.1 chunked bodies skipped the 1 MB cap and Starlette could buffer without bound.

- New outermost ASGI `RequestBodySizeLimitMiddleware` (`api/request_body_limit.py`): fast-reject oversized `Content-Length`; for missing length, count real `http.request` bytes, disconnect the stream, and replace the inner response with **413**.
- Does **not** raise out of `receive()` — Starlette maps that to HTTP 400 (`There was an error parsing the body`).
- Tests: Content-Length 413 (existing), chunked ASGI helper without `Content-Length`, streamed TestClient body → 413.

## Test plan
- [x] `./scripts/quick-test.sh --path tests/test_security.py --keyword request_body_size`
- [x] `./scripts/check-all.sh` (exit 0)
- [ ] GitHub **Cursor Bugbot** completed analysis (not usage-limit skip)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches API request handling at the outermost middleware layer (DoS mitigation), but behavior is narrowly scoped to the existing 1 MB cap with regression tests and no auth/data-model changes.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Closes #1558.** The old `request_body_size_middleware` only read `Content-Length`, so chunked or length-less bodies could bypass the 1 MB limit and let Starlette buffer unbounded data.
> 
> The PR moves enforcement to **`RequestBodySizeLimitMiddleware`** in `api/request_body_limit.py`, registered as the **outermost** layer via `app.add_middleware` so byte counting happens before the framework parses JSON/forms. Oversized declared length still gets an immediate **413**; streaming bodies accumulate `http.request` bytes, disconnect when over cap, and respond with the same JSON **413** body—without raising from `receive()` (which Starlette would turn into **400**).
> 
> **SECURITY** docs (EN/pt-BR) and the dashboard access-control plan now describe actual-byte counting and point at the new module. **`tests/test_security.py`** adds chunked ASGI coverage plus a streamed TestClient case alongside the existing Content-Length test.

author: kent-tokyo
body:
Follow-up to #49 (merged \`5ec4361\`).

## What I found after merging #49

CodeQL re-scanned the merged commit and **still flags all 9** original \`py/path-injection\` alerts, now at shifted line numbers but the same underlying lines. Checked \`most_recent_instance.commit_sha\` on one directly — it's genuinely scanning \`5ec4361\`, the fix-containing commit. The basename-only guard (\`os.path.basename(run_id) != run_id\`) is a **real, empirically verified sanitizer** (proven in #49's own leaked-fixture test), but CodeQL's taint tracker doesn't recognize that specific pattern as a barrier.

While rewriting it into the more standard, CodeQL-recognized shape, I also found a **sibling instance of the same bug**: \`get_pipeline_review\` (reached via \`GET /api/review?kind=pipeline&run=...\`, a different route than \`/api/pipeline\` — not among the 12 originally flagged lines) has the identical unguarded \`os.path.join(DATA_DIR, "runs", run_id)\`.

## The fix

1. Replaced the basename-only check with the canonical \`os.path.realpath()\` + \`startswith(base + os.sep)\` containment check — the standard idiom, and it also closes a symlink-based escape the basename check alone didn't cover.
2. Extracted this into one shared \`_resolve_pipeline_run_dir(run_id)\` helper, used by both \`get_pipeline_status\` and (now) \`get_pipeline_review\`.

## Verification

- Reverted the helper to the unguarded join and confirmed **both** \`get_pipeline_status("..")\` and \`get_pipeline_review("..")\` bypass validation and reach content outside \`data/runs/\` — one directly leaks the planted \`{"leaked": true}\` fixture, the other proceeds past the traversal instead of returning \`None\`. Restored the fix and reran to confirm both pass again.
- \`python3 scripts/test_gate_dashboard.py\`: 35/35 passing (33 existing + 2 new \`PipelineReviewPathTraversalTests\`; #49's 8 \`PipelineStatusPathTraversalTests\` already cover the realpath-based rewrite since they test the same public function).
- \`python3 -m py_compile\`: clean
- \`cargo fmt\`/\`clippy\` pre-commit hook: clean (unrelated Python-only change, ran anyway)

I'll check after this merges whether CodeQL's alert count actually drops this time — if the realpath+prefix pattern still isn't recognized, the remaining path is dismissing the alerts with this PR's verification as the documented reason, same as the 3 already-identified false positives in \`start_run\`.

author: nekodas-neko
body:
Docs-only. Three entries, filed after Q-419 in the queue.

> **Stacked on #249.** Until that merges, this diff also shows Q-419. Both are docs-only.

## Q-420 — session RPE is asked for in a unit the owner cannot judge

Owner, unprompted: *"i cant tell session rpe I can tell excefcise rpe; so maybe it takes the average of excercise RPE to calculate the sessionnrpe and it can be overwritten if needed."*

Measured in production (the owner's own rows):

| | rated | total | fill |
|---|---|---|---|
| `workout_sessions.session_rpe` | 20 | 78 completed | **25.6%** |
| `set_logs.rpe` | 625 | 1,047 | **59.7%** |

**24 completed sessions carry rated sets and no session RPE** — deriving takes coverage from 20 to 44 with no new tapping.

**Why this is a prerequisite, not a parallel item:** Q-419 teaches the day's energy budget to read session RPE. Three sessions in four have none, so Q-419 is largely inert until this lands.

**The entry does not treat "take the average" as obviously correct.** Two problems it names:

- **The scales don't match.** The per-set strip offers 6–10; the session grid offers 1–10; `intensityFromRpe` calls ≤4 easy. A mean of set ratings **can never reach the easy tier** — the floor is 6 — so an identity mapping silently deletes one of three intensity tiers and biases every derived session upward.
- **They measure different things.** Per-set RPE is proximity to failure on that set; session RPE is global exertion, which carries volume and duration. Three sets at RPE 9 and twenty sets at RPE 9 average identically.

**There is a calibration set, and it is encouraging but not clean.** 20 sessions carry both:

| owner's session RPE | n | mean set RPE | max set RPE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 3 | 7.15 | 7.67 |
| 8 | 15 | 7.41 | 8.53 |
| 9 | 2 | 8.25 | 10.00 |

The mean tracks the owner's own rating monotonically — but in the dominant bucket **7.41 rounds to 7 where the owner said 8**, and one point at the 8 boundary is a whole intensity tier. n = 20, so the entry says fit something simple and don't tune a curve to it.

The override the owner asked for needs provenance stored (`session_rpe` is a bare nullable integer today), so it carries a schema change — **Lane A**.

## Q-421 — the accurate model is already here and has no callers

The MET formula in use is documented as **Oura's fallback** for when there isn't enough motion signal. The primary path is a neural model already vendored, listed in `model-files.json`, downloaded at runtime and unit-tested — and **its only caller in the repo is its own test file**. The module header names the gap: *"Assembling the feature vector from motion/steps/HR is a separate step."*

The inputs exist too: `workout_hr_stats` 77 rows (42 with `avg_bpm`), `set_hr_stats` 709 rows, `daily_zone_minutes` 78 days, with HR reserve already computed (maxHr 187 / restingHr 53) and already trusted by Readiness and Activity. The calorie estimator is the only consumer ignoring it.

Recommends the closed-form HR estimator **first** (no model, no feature vector, immediately better than duration × MET) and the ONNX path only once the feature layout is read from the pinned model source — never guessed. Flags that `running_baselines` is empty in production, so max/resting HR must not be sourced there.

## Q-422 — calibrate against the owner's own energy balance

`adaptive-tdee` already back-solves maintenance from intake and weight. It calibrates the *day*, not the workout; the residual is what a per-user multiplier should be fitted to. The entry writes down the three ways that fit goes wrong: **identifiability** (separate strength/cardio/step multipliers aren't recoverable from one scalar residual), **under-logging** (Q-387 measured six partial days moving maintenance 514 kcal — the same mechanism moves a multiplier silently), and **circularity** (fit against weight, which is exogenous, not the app's own targets).

Routed per CLAUDE.md: Tuning proposes, owner signs off, Lane A implements.

## Verification

`pnpm check:rules` — 50 of 50. Production figures came from the read-only `claude_ro` endpoint; **every count above is the owner's own rows only**, which is the right scope here since the owner is the reporter. Docs-only diff; no runtime surfaces exercised.
